DeAmazoning - I hacked my Kindle, Alexa, and soon Firestick

Published on 2026-01-31 at 20:37 UTC+12 by Oscar N.
Alexa Echo Show 5 Gen2 + Kindle 5th Gen, both deamazoned

Pre-Process

As I'm sure many people are waking up to, Amazon is not a good company. They give us convenience at the cost of their workers and our privacy. Dodgy partnerships, mass surveillance, and Amazon workers having to pee in bottles or risk being fired are the very tip of the iceberg when it comes to this oligarch run company. I won't use the term 'giving credit where it's due' for Amazon because a company like theirs deserves no credit. Instead I simply acknowledge that for a company to do bad things well, it has to manufacture it's things well too. The Kindle, Alexa, and Firestick are three of Amazons biggest products and are no exception.

It would be a waste to simply contribute to the growing land fill with these products when we can liberate them from Amazon and make them much more useful then they ever were before, all while no longer playing into Amazons' hand. In this post, I write about my experience 'unlocking' both the Kindle 5th Gen, and the Alexa Echo Show 5 2nd Gen (I have an old Firestick but haven't attempted to work at that yet as mine may have updated to the point where I can not hack it).

In-Process

Thankfully lots of people like their Amazon devices but hate the 'Amazon' aspect of them (the operating systems, the restrictions, the lack of privacy) and so there is this massive community dedicated to working out how to hack into these devices and also how to replicate this for the average joe. When it came to unlocking BOTH of these devices I actually watched the two different YouTube videos from the same creator, DammitJeff. 

For the Alexa, developers exploited vulnerabilities in the MediaTek chips (using a tool called amonet-checkers) to completely unlock the bootloader. What this means is that when you turn on your Alexa, it automatically selects the operating system to load into, and people found away to unlock this allowing us to add different operating systems and even completely wipe Amazon's Fire OS and flash a Custom ROM (which is what I did to say good bye to Amazon as much as much I can). The most popular operating replacement I've seen so far for the Alexa is LineageOS which is an open-source version of Android. After following the steps DammitJeff instructed, I was then able to have full access to the android system including the Google Play Store, which allows the freedom to chose your own personal assistants, and to run your own self-hosted smart home apps like Home Assistant (which is what I am using my unlocked Alexa for, to have a nice little display for my HA dashboard).

For the Kindle, developers have found software exploits, an example being through the ads Amazon shows on the Kindle (which is so ironic to use force-fed ads on a device we already paid for to exploit it and gain freedom from said ads + extra benefits).  How this differs from unlocking the Alexa is that this jailbreak does not allow us to replace the Kindles' OS. It does, however, allow us to install third-party apps and plug-ins like KOReader (basically a liberating document viewer that allows you to read your own 'legally sourced' books without having to pay Amazon for a license to the book). It also allows users to add custom screensavers, bypass Amazon's book DRM limitations, and block forced over-the-air software updates.

Now, instead of being forced to purchase books through Amazons' Kindle Store, I can download my own books from various sources, and simply plug in my Kindle to my laptop and drag them over like a normal USB. Due to the large community backing this, people have also managed to allow users to upload their books wirelessly, which gives you a much closer-to-original experience while still having a Kindle that less tied down. I even managed to play chess on it.

Post-Process

To be honest, unlocking both of these devices was really easy, and the YouTubers who make videos explaining how to do it explain the steps in such an easily understandable way. My use cases now for the Kindle and Alexa are infinite in comparison to the fixed use cases. Ultimately, I think if companies are going to get greedier and greedier people are just going to come up with more ways to use the tech against them and more for ourselves. As I learn to unlock more Amazon devices and build my own 'unlocked ex-Amazon ecosystem' I'll do more posts on the ONWiki, so stay tuned.
